record.paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
record.context_brief: Fundamental limits in measuring stellar mass and star formation rate
record.original_question: For galaxies observed over a wide range of redshifts and halo masses, can astronomers reduce the systematic uncertainties involved in converting observed spectra or broadband photometry into stellar mass, meaning the total mass in stars, and star formation rate, meaning the rate at which stellar mass grows through star formation; or are standard methods reaching a fundamental limit in how accurately these quantities can be measured and used to improve galaxy-formation theory?

evidence.quote: Two of the most fundamental parameters that describe a galaxy are its total mass in stars, and the rate at which stellar mass grows via star formation, the star formation rate (SFR).
Can we really develop techniques to reduce systematic uncertainties in deriving key quantities such as stellar mass and SFRs, or are we truly reaching a fundamental limit in our ability to do so?

artifact.category_tag: galaxy stellar mass and SFR estimation
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the inverse problem of estimating two fundamental quantities of a galaxy from observational data:

(i) the stellar mass M⋆, defined as the total mass currently locked in stars in the galaxy, and
(ii) the star formation rate (SFR), defined as the rate (in solar masses per unit time) at which new stellar mass is being produced by ongoing star formation.

The available data consist either of an observed galaxy spectrum or of broadband photometric fluxes in a finite set of bands, observed at a known redshift z. Standard estimators map this data to (M⋆, SFR) via stellar population synthesis: one assumes a stellar initial mass function, a parametric or non-parametric star formation history, a metallicity evolution, a dust attenuation law, and (where relevant) a model of nebular emission and AGN contamination, then fits the predicted spectral energy distribution to the data.

Question: Across a broad range of redshifts z and host halo masses M_h, is it possible in principle to construct estimators of M⋆ and SFR whose systematic uncertainties (arising from the choice of IMF, star formation history parametrization, dust law, metallicity, stellar evolution tracks, and nebular/AGN contributions) can be made arbitrarily small with improved modeling and data, or is there a fundamental floor on the achievable systematic accuracy of these two quantities when inferred from spectra or broadband photometry? Quantify, if possible, this floor, and determine whether it is small enough that the inferred (M⋆, SFR) can meaningfully discriminate between competing theories of galaxy formation and evolution.
artifact.status_search_result: This is an open conceptual/methodological question in extragalactic astrophysics. Recent SED-fitting reviews (e.g., Conroy 2013; Pacifici et al. 2023) and JWST-era studies continue to report systematic uncertainties of order 0.2–0.3 dex in stellar mass and significantly larger in SFR depending on assumptions, with no consensus that a hard fundamental floor has been established or eliminated. The problem remains active and unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Modeling the Panchromatic Spectral Energy Distributions of Galaxies (Conroy 2013)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews systematic uncertainties in stellar masses and SFRs derived from SED fitting, identifying IMF, SFH, dust, and stellar evolution as dominant sources of uncertainty.
status_evidence.claim: Systematic uncertainties in M⋆ and SFR from SED fitting remain a major open issue.

status_evidence.title: Pacifici et al. 2023, The Art of Measuring Physical Parameters in Galaxies
status_evidence.snippet: Comparison of 14 SED-fitting codes shows scatter of ~0.1–0.3 dex in stellar mass and larger in SFR, with systematic offsets persisting across methods.
status_evidence.claim: State-of-the-art comparison shows persistent systematic floors in derived M⋆ and SFR.
